comments.author: @rayhallett
comments.text:
I have sailed (and paddled) the eastern end of Lake Ontario for over 50 years. I even knew some of the old river pilots and fishing boat crews, fellows now long gone. We could all talk about the sudden dark line that one could see coming across the lake towards you. It was time to reef sail and get below. A furious squall would roar in, lashing you with rain or hail and whipping the water into a froth of waves, tossing our boats about, shipping water. And then, in a instant, it had passed and a brief calm would ensue. It could come on a sunny or rainy day (there would also have to be some clouds), or out of the dark, at night.  I have also seen our compass become a little uncertain once--and it was over the Charity Shoal.
And the eastern end of Lake Ontario does shape the prevailing winds, the waves and the currents that have had the whole length of the lake to cross before hitting these narrows.
But, it was great to have your read on all these stories. Usually, YouTube channels will exploit the "mystery" and not the facts when it comes to tales like this. You did a great job.
I do think people need to pay attention to the waters (and shoals) around here and would be better served studying winds and squalls than malevolent forces at work.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: This is exactly the kind of firsthand context I love seeing in the comments. That description of the dark line and the squall rolling across the lake really brings the danger into focus. And I agree, the weather, shoals, currents and geography are interesting enough without forcing a supernatural explanation. Thanks for adding this.

comments.author: @themittonmethod1243
comments.text: we call them the "great lakes".. they are properly regarded as inland seas... they have all the same features of oceans - tides, long fetch where the winds can (and do) whip up the swells, shoals, fog and other inclement weather... do not be fooled by their moniker... they are big waters.. Cheers, Mates.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Absolutely. The Great Lakes really can behave like inland seas, especially with their long fetch, sudden storms, heavy swells, fog, and dangerous shoals. The one small distinction is that their astronomical tides are tiny compared with the oceans; most noticeable water-level swings come from wind and weather. Either way, definitely not waters to underestimate. Cheers!

comments.text: BAVARIA  SEAMAN ABANDONNED SHIP AND SUBSEQUENTLY  DROWNED IN THE LAKE ONTARIO

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Exactly. The Bavaria itself survived the storm, but the crew abandoned her in the yawlboat, which later capsized. That’s what makes the story so tragic, they left the ship trying to survive, and the smaller boat was what ultimately doomed them.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Most of the documented wrecks are older commercial vessels like schooners, steamers, and freighters. I haven’t found a reliable breakdown showing exactly how many were recreational boats, so I don’t want to guess. Good question though!
